notes.meaning: The Lord spoke to Moses from inside the newly built Tent of Meeting, which served as His dwelling place among His people. Moses had been waiting outside because God's bright glory filled the tent, so the Lord called out to invite him to listen. Instead of speaking with thunder from the mountain, God spoke gently from the mercy seat to teach Israel how to worship Him.

Moses was told to give instructions to all the people of Israel about bringing gifts to God. The Lord allowed them to bring animals from their own herds of cattle or flocks of sheep and goats. Because these tame animals were part of a family's daily livelihood, giving one up meant the sacrifice cost the worshipper something real.

If someone brought a bull as a burnt offering, the animal had to be a healthy male without any blemish or defect. The worshipper brought it right to the entrance of the courtyard near the altar so God would accept it. This flawless animal pictured the complete purity of Jesus Christ, who offered Himself willingly for sinners.

The worshipper pressed a hand onto the head of the animal before it was killed. This action showed that the person was dedicating the animal to God and asking Him to let it stand in their place. In this way, the sacrifice made atonement, meaning it covered the person's sin so they could be at peace with God.

differ.view: The burnt offering made atonement sacramentally, serving as a sacred sign that pointed the worshipper's faith forward to the true sacrifice of Christ.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The Hebrew word translated as make atonement originally meant to wipe clean or purge, or to win someone over with a gift.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The burnt offering served to honor God's supreme authority, brought acceptance and expiation for the worshipper, and prefigured the sacrifice of Christ.

notes.meaning: The worshipper killed the young bull before the Lord, acknowledging that human sin deserves death. Then Aaron's sons, the priests, caught the blood and splashed it against every side of the bronze altar. Splashing the blood showed that a life had been given up to bring reconciliation with God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Early Greek translations describe the priests, rather than the worshipper, performing the slaughter of the animal.

notes.meaning: The animal was skinned and cut neatly into pieces along its joints. Removing the hide prepared the meat cleanly, and the skin was later given to the priest. Cutting the sacrifice into pieces prepared it to be burned completely on the altar.

The priests tended the fire on the bronze altar and carefully stacked the wood in order. This fire originally came down from heaven and was never supposed to go out. Serving God required careful attention and obedience to His commands.

The priests arranged the pieces of meat, including the head and the fat, on top of the burning wood. Laying every part in an orderly way showed that the entire animal was dedicated to the Lord. The fat helped fuel the flames so the whole offering was consumed.

The internal parts and legs were thoroughly washed with water before being placed on the fire. The priest then burned everything on the altar as a pleasing aroma to the Lord. God took pleasure not in the smell of burning meat itself, but in the humble, obedient heart of the worshipper and the promise of Christ to come.

differ.view: The burning of the offering did not show God consuming the victim in wrath, but rather His gracious acceptance of a dedicated life after forgiveness had been granted.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The Hebrew phrase traditionally translated as an offering made by fire is better understood as simply meaning a gift.

notes.meaning: A worshipper could also bring a male sheep or goat without any blemish if they could not afford a bull. Like the larger offering, it had to be healthy and whole to honor the Lord properly. God looks at the devotion of the giver rather than the size of the gift.

The animal was to be killed on the north side of the altar before the Lord. Aaron's sons gathered the blood and dashed it against all sides of the altar. The north side of the courtyard provided an open, convenient space for the priests to do this sacred work.

The animal was cut into its pieces, and the priest arranged them, along with the head and the fat, on the wood on the altar. Treating every piece with order and care showed respect for God. This complete dedication represented the worshipper giving their whole life over to God's service.

The internal parts and legs were washed with clean water, and the priest burned the entire animal on the altar. It rose as a sweet aroma that was pleasing to the Lord. Washing the sacrifice reminded the people that approaching a pure God requires clean hearts and holy living.

People who were too poor to afford a sheep or goat were permitted to bring a turtledove or a young pigeon. These birds were gentle, harmless, and common enough for anyone to obtain. God made this provision so that no one, no matter how poor, was shut out from coming to His altar.

The priest took the bird to the altar and pinched off its head, placing it immediately on the fire. Because a small bird has very little blood, its blood was drained directly against the side of the altar instead of being collected in a bowl. Even this small offering received the full care of God's priest.

The priest removed the bird's digestive crop with its filthy contents and tossed it into the ash heap on the east side of the altar. The east side was farthest from the Most Holy Place and closest to the gate where waste was carried outside the camp. This act showed that impurities must be put away when coming into God's presence.

The priest tore the bird open by its wings without ripping it completely in half, and then burned it on the altar fire. Even though this was the simple offering of a poor person, the Lord called it a pleasing aroma, just like the costly bull. God values the sincere faith of the giver far more than the price of the gift.
